feed.title: Self-Hosting & Personal Cloud — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: An annotated directory of links on software, AI, security and science. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Awesome DigitalOcean
entry.summary: A list of tools and guides for the DigitalOcean cloud platform.

entry.title: Awesome Heroku
entry.summary: A list of add-ons, buildpacks and resources for the Heroku PaaS.

entry.title: Awesome Home Assistant
entry.summary: A list of add-ons, components and dashboards for Home Assistant, the open-source home automation platform. Unlike the official integrations it gathers community-made custom components and automations.

entry.title: DigitalOcean
entry.summary: A developer-friendly cloud server (droplet) provider with simple pricing.

entry.title: DreamHost
entry.summary: High-availability shared and cloud web hosting.

entry.title: Heroku
entry.summary: A platform-as-a-service that deploys code instantly on a git push.

entry.title: Hostinger
entry.summary: Affordable shared and cloud web hosting.

entry.title: InfinityFree
entry.summary: Completely free web hosting with PHP and MySQL support.

entry.title: Surge
entry.summary: Free hosting that publishes static sites with a single command.

entry.title: Awesome-Selfhosted
entry.summary: The canonical, categorised list of free-software services you can host on your own server. Unlike the raw GitHub list its browsable site filters every entry by licence, language and whether it is still active — the standard place to find an alternative without depending on a cloud service.

entry.title: Geek Cookbook
entry.summary: End-to-end recipes for building a highly-available “private cloud” on Docker Swarm. Unlike Awesome-Selfhosted’s list approach it gives step-by-step deployment: not which software to pick, but how to stand up the one you picked in production.

entry.title: selfh.st
entry.summary: A newsletter and content site rounding up weekly news, new software and updates from the self-hosting world. Unlike static lists it is a feed: a live, dated source for tracking what launched and what was updated.

entry.title: YunoHost
entry.summary: A project that turns your own server into an operating system with one-click app installs. Unlike setting up Docker by hand it abstracts the admin: you manage users, domains and backups from one panel, and catalog apps install in a single step.

entry.title: AdGuard Home
entry.summary: A network-wide blocker doing the same job as Pi-hole; what differs is that it ships its own DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS server and lets you write per-client rules. One binary, no extra dependencies.

entry.title: Audiobookshelf
entry.summary: A self-hosted server for managing and streaming your audiobook and podcast collection, with progress synced across devices. Unlike Plex or Jellyfin it is built for audiobooks specifically, so chapter marks, playback speed and series tracking behave properly.

entry.title: Dawarich
entry.summary: Self-hosted location history with a map view, able to import a Google Location History export. The difference from Google’s own service is that the data stays with you — and does not vanish when the product is discontinued.

entry.title: Element
entry.summary: A messaging client on the Matrix protocol, with end-to-end encryption and federation between servers. That federation is the break from Slack or Discord: two people on different servers share a room without a single company in the middle.

entry.title: Immich
entry.summary: A self-hosted answer to Google Photos: background upload from the phone, face recognition, map and timeline. What separates it from other self-hosted galleries is that the mobile app actually backs up in the background, which most of them never manage.

entry.title: LibreOffice
entry.summary: An office suite of writer, spreadsheet, presentation and database, defaulting to the open ODF standard. The difference from Microsoft Office is licensing and data ownership; the price is occasional layout drift on complex .docx files.

entry.title: Logseq
entry.summary: An outliner with bi-directional links that keeps every note as a plain Markdown file on disk. Against Notion the data is in your folder; against Obsidian the primary unit is the block rather than the page, which suits daily journalling better.

entry.title: Nextcloud
entry.summary: A self-hosted file sync and collaboration suite: calendar, contacts, document editing, chat. Where Syncthing only syncs, this adds a web interface and share links — it is aiming at Google Workspace rather than at Dropbox.

entry.title: Organic Maps
entry.summary: An offline map and navigation app on OpenStreetMap data, with no trackers and no ads. It is the fork Maps.me spawned when that went commercial — the continuation of the version people actually liked.

entry.title: Pi-hole
entry.summary: A network-wide ad blocker that runs as your DNS server and sinkholes ad and tracker domains. Unlike a browser extension it also covers smart TVs, phone apps and IoT devices — everything you cannot install an extension on.

entry.title: Rocket.Chat
entry.summary: A self-hostable team messaging platform with channels, threads, voice and bridges. Against Slack, the data stays on your infrastructure and message history is not locked behind a paid tier.

entry.title: Syncthing
entry.summary: Continuous file synchronisation between devices with no central server: the devices talk directly. Unlike Dropbox no copy ever reaches a cloud, and there is no storage quota — you have as much room as you have disk.

entry.title: Thunderbird
entry.summary: A desktop mail client under the Mozilla umbrella, with IMAP, calendar, contacts and OpenPGP signing in one place. Against webmail, the archive lives on your disk and stays yours when you change provider.

entry.title: Appwrite
entry.summary: An open-source backend-as-a-service offering auth, database, storage and functions, self-hostable.

entry.title: CapRover
entry.summary: A free, self-hosted PaaS for one-click apps and Docker deploys on your own server.

entry.title: Cloudron
entry.summary: Self-hosts web apps with managed updates, backups and single sign-on.

entry.title: Coolify
entry.summary: An open-source self-hosted PaaS you run on your own server — a self-hosted alternative to Heroku/Netlify.

entry.title: Deno Deploy
entry.summary: A platform that runs JavaScript/TypeScript serverless on a global edge network.

entry.title: Dokku
entry.summary: The smallest open-source Heroku-like PaaS, running on a single host via git push.

entry.title: Feedly
entry.summary: An RSS reader where you decide what you read at the source level, unlike algorithmic feeds — and nothing you have not read disappears.

entry.title: Fly.io
entry.summary: Runs app containers at edge locations close to users, with global deploy, Postgres and volumes.

entry.title: Koyeb
entry.summary: Deploys apps and containers globally, git-driven and serverless with scale-to-zero.

entry.title: Linode (Akamai)
entry.summary: A developer-friendly VPS cloud with predictably priced Linux virtual machines.

entry.title: Netlify
entry.summary: Hosting for modern static and JAMstack sites with git-push deploys, edge, forms and functions.

entry.title: PikaPods
entry.summary: Managed hosting that runs open-source apps without you administering a server.

entry.title: Railway
entry.summary: Infrastructure that deploys apps and databases from git with minimal configuration, instantly.

entry.title: Render
entry.summary: A unified cloud for web services, static sites and databases with Heroku-like simplicity.
